summary: Children justify WHY addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations — the step from executing a strategy to explaining it. Two justifications are central: partitioning ('add tens and ones separately, then recombine') is valid because a number is composed of tens and ones and addends may be split, reordered and regrouped without changing the total (commutativity/associativity); and compensation ('add 100 for 99, then subtract 1') is an equivalent transformation — you adjusted by a known amount and undo the surplus. The target is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers. A dialogic 'prove-it' routine is well-suited as the primary vehicle because producing a justification requires the child to articulate their reasoning, which an open spoken exchange is well-suited to elicit; written annotation, manipulatives and spot-the-flaw tasks serve as complementary scaffolds and probes.
misconceptions: Restating the procedure or citing authority ('the teacher said') instead of giving a reason
Doubting that splitting/reordering preserves the total (fearing something is lost when a number is broken up)
Compensation direction error: adding 100 for 99 then adding 1 (not seeing 100 is one too many)
Explaining WHAT was done but not WHY it is valid

activities.title: Talk with a 'prove-it' partner who never accepts a bare rule
steps: Solve 46 + 37 by adding tens and ones separately (40 + 30 = 70, 6 + 7 = 13, 70 + 13 = 83), then say the answer aloud.

When your partner (teacher, peer, or an in-role character) asks 'but why doesn't breaking 46 into 40 and 6 lose anything?', explain in your own words why splitting and recombining keeps the same total.
Try splitting 37 a different way — e.g. 35 + 2 instead of 30 + 7 — and explain whether the method still works and why, to show the reasoning transfers to a new split.
Solve 46 + 99 by adding 100 and then adjusting; when asked 'why take one BACK rather than add one?', explain how much too much 100 is compared with 99 and why the surplus must be removed.
Respond to a counterexample your partner offers (e.g. a friend who split 46 into 40 + 6 but only added the 40 and forgot the 6) and say whether that mistake means splitting itself is unreliable.
activities.insight: A remembered procedure becomes an owned explanation: the number IS its tens and ones, so like parts can be added and recombined without loss, and this holds whichever way you split; adding 100 for 99 adds exactly one too many, so you subtract one to land on adding exactly 99.

activities.title: Show the whole is conserved: partition with materials, compensate on a number line
steps: Using base-ten blocks, a part-whole diagram, or a bar model, split 46 into 40 + 6 and check that the pieces still make 46 — nothing is lost when you break it up.
Rearrange the order and grouping of the parts (e.g. 6 + 40, or group the tens first) and confirm the total is unchanged.
On a number line, add 46 + 99 by jumping 100 forward, then step back 1; highlight the extra +1 you overshot by.
Say out loud why you step back rather than forward.
activities.insight: Partitioning preserves the total because the parts still compose the same whole and any order/grouping of addends gives the same sum; compensation is 'overshoot then step back' by the known surplus.

activities.title: Annotate a worked strategy with the reason for each step
steps: Take a written worked method for 46 + 37 (40 + 30 = 70; 6 + 7 = 13; 70 + 13 = 83).
Label each step with WHY it is allowed, not just what was done (e.g. '46 is 40 and 6', 'the order of adding the parts doesn't change the total', 'recombining the parts gives the whole').
Do the same for a compensation method (46 + 99 = 46 + 100 − 1) and name the surplus of one and its undoing.
activities.insight: Every step of a strategy has a place-value reason; a justification names those reasons, not just the actions.

activities.title: Spot the flawed reasoning / pick the valid justification
steps: Read two or three explanations of a compensation step and choose the one that correctly justifies subtracting 1 after adding 100.
Find the error in a written reasoning chain (e.g. one that adds 1 instead of subtracting it) and say what has gone wrong.
Explain in your own words why the correct justification is correct.
activities.insight: Recognising valid versus invalid reasoning sharpens the child's sense of what counts as a justification, especially the forced direction of the compensation adjustment.

checkQuestion: Discuss, don't mark: 'When you add 46 + 37 by working out 40 + 30 = 70 and 6 + 7 = 13 and then combining, why is it OK to break the numbers up like that and still get the right total?' Then: 'To add 46 + 99, someone adds 100 and then takes 1 away — why is that allowed, and how do they know to take 1 away rather than add it?' Listen for place-value and properties reasoning.
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning: splitting works because 46 is 40+6 and 37 is 30+7, and addends can be split, reordered and regrouped without changing the total, so adding like parts and recombining gives the same whole. Compensation works because 100 is one more than 99, so adding 100 adds one too many and you subtract one to get back to adding exactly 99 — an equivalent transformation.
